newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS -- ends mostly unchanged.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS -- ends mostly unchanged.

text.p: U.S. municipal bonds were mostly unchanged in late Wednesday action, with slight weakness at the long end, market participants said.
"There were a lot of bid-wanted accounts, and we're getting good bids," one trader said. The trader said a key focus of the day was Washington, D.C.'s $234 million competitive offering.
Lehman Brothers won the issue and reoffered the 2026 term bonds at 6.20 percent. A source familiar with the issue said most of it had been sold.
Raymond James & Associates topped off the $429 million negotiated calendar with a $104 million Pasco County, Fla., deal. The firm priced the bonds at a top yield of 5.675 percent in 2011.
Municipal prices followed the Treasury market throughout the day. The government long bond was unchanged in late New York trading at 94-31/32, after showing gains at midday.

Low supply continues to be the dominant market force for munis. Municipal bond sales for Thursday are expected to total $793 million in 25 sales, according to Reuters Municipal Bond Information Group.

Negotiated offerings total $414 million in 10 sales, with a $144 million Dallas-Fort Worth, Texas, deal through Bear, Stearns & Co., Inc. topping the list. Standard & Poor's raised its rating on the airport Wednesday to A-plus from single-A. On the competitive side, 15 sales totaling $380 million are on the schedule. A $256 million Los Angeles County MTA, Calif., deal at 1200 EDT is the largest.
June municipal futures rose 1/32 Wednesday to close at 116-3/32, while June Treasury futures were unchanged at 108-23/32. The MOB spread between the two contracts widened one tick to 236.
In the secondary market, Denver Airport MBIA 5-1/2s of 2025 were bid at 5.79 percent, down one basis point after showing an unchanged bid in morning action.
Cleveland AMBAC 5-1/4 COPs of 2022 were bid at 5.67 percent, down three basis points.

In early economic data Wednesday, the Commerce Department reported strong demand for new transportation equipment, which helped drive durable goods orders for April up 1.4 percent to a seasonally adjusted $175.56 billion.
The figure marked the third increase in the past four months. It was slightly higher than the 1.3 percent estimate predicted by a Reuters poll of economists.
